text:
Predicates:
Taller(x, y) ::: x is taller than y.
CanBlock(x, y) ::: x can block y's shooting.
Jump(x) ::: x can jump when shooting.
GreatShooter(x) ::: x is a great shooter.
Michael ::: Michael (constant).
Windy ::: Windy (constant).
Person(x) ::: x is a person.
Class(x) ::: x is in Michael's class.
Premises:
∀x ∀y (Person(x) ∧ Person(y) ∧ Taller(x, y) → CanBlock(x, y)) ::: If one man is taller than another, he can block his shooting.
Taller(Michael, y) ∀y (Person(y) ∧ Class(y) → Taller(Michael, y)) ::: Michael is taller than everyone in his class.
Taller(x, y) ∧ Taller(y, z) → Taller(x, z) ::: Transitivity of taller relation.
Taller(Peter, Michael) ::: Peter is taller than Michael.
CanBlock(Michael, y) ← ¬Jump(y) ::: Michael can block y's shooting if y cannot jump.
¬CanBlock(Windy, Michael) ::: Michael cannot block Windy's shooting.
Jump(x) → GreatShooter(x) ::: Anyone who can jump when shooting is a great shooter.
Conclusion:
Taller(Peter, y) ∧ Class(y) → Taller(Peter, y) ::: If Peter is taller than someone in Michael's class, then Peter is taller than that person.  
(Alternatively, since the statement is about Peter being shorter than someone in Michael's class, the logical focus is on the possible comparison; but per the data, the question is whether Peter is shorter than someone in the class, which is uncertain, thus the conclusion remains uncertain.)
